description: An independent participant interested in engineering, science, and creative problem-solving. Participating in NASA Space Apps to apply research and design skills, explore new ideas and develop a thoughtful response to a real-world challenge.
summary:
OrbitO₂ is a prototype that helps astronauts log blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂) and pulse and review those readings alongside mission activities and environment changes. Our demo follows Bob, a fictional mission specialist on day 215 of HORIZON-365. When Bob records a check-in, the app saves what he was doing, where he was, and whether he recently changed environments. Each saved reading appears on an interactive timeline and can be reviewed alongside nearby mission events.

NASA’s human spaceflight hazards framework informed what the app asks crew members to log. An airlock pressure example from NASA’s International Space Station Familiarization Manual gives Bob’s simulated scenario a concrete reference point.

A single reading tells a crew member what was measured. The surrounding context helps them decide what to compare, recheck, or share. OrbitO₂ carries that context into two 48-hour reports: a plain-language briefing for the astronaut and a detailed record for a health professional.
details:
The problem and intended impact

A blood oxygen reading is more useful when the person reviewing it knows what was happening at the time. An astronaut might record a reading after exercise, during recovery, or after moving between environments. Days later, it can be hard to reconstruct those details from a number and a timestamp alone.

We built OrbitO₂ to capture that context during the check-in, while it’s still fresh. Our goal is to help crew members make more informed comparisons, identify readings worth rechecking, and share a more complete record with a health professional. The prototype demonstrates this workflow through Bob, a fictional mission specialist on day 215 of HORIZON-365.

How it works

A crew member can enter readings manually, connect a supported Bluetooth pulse oximeter, or scan a QR code to try the phone sensor. The phone camera estimates pulse by looking for repeating changes in fingertip brightness. SpO₂ is simulated in phone mode. Each check-in can include location, activity, symptoms, and a recent environment change.

Saved check-ins become points on two charts, one for SpO₂ and one for pulse. OrbitO₂ places each point according to its timestamp and logged value, and breaks the line when readings are at least 2½ hours apart. Selecting a point opens the original log. Fixed rules explain why a value was flagged and surface details such as poor signal quality. The same logs generate two downloadable 48-hour PDFs: a plain-language astronaut briefing and a health professional report with individual reading details.

What’s creative about it

Compare Events gives each selected mission event its own minute zero. That lets a crew member compare check-ins from different parts of the mission on the same time scale. For example, Bob’s 16:35 UTC reading appears 35 minutes after the 16:00 airlock event. The same reading can also be viewed relative to a nearby exercise event. Showing both time relationships alongside activity and signal quality helps the reviewer see why several explanations may need to be considered. Timing alone cannot establish a cause.

How NASA resources informed the design

NASA’s 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight identifies closed or hostile environments as a hazard. That informed the fields we added to the Oxygen Log, including the crew member’s current location, previous location, and time since the transition. NASA Human Research Program

We also used the 10.2 psi airlock preparation example referenced in NASA’s International Space Station Familiarization Manual. OrbitO₂ converts it to approximately 70.3 kPa and displays it on Bob’s fictional airlock event. The pressure is a NASA reference value. Bob’s mission events and health readings are simulated. NASA Technical Reports Server

What we built with and what we considered

We started the prototype in Google AI Studio with Gemini and continued development in React, TypeScript, and Vite. We used Web Bluetooth for compatible pulse oximeters, browser camera APIs for the phone pulse demo, and pdf-lib for report exports. The app uses fixed rules to generate reading explanations and report summaries during use.

We designed for measurement problems and limited time. If Bluetooth or the phone sensor fails, a crew member can finish with manual entry. The log preserves the measurement source and signal quality so those details remain visible during review. We labelled simulated data and configured demo targets throughout the prototype. For judges, we included a guided walkthrough and Explore shortcuts to the NASA examples, the flagged reading, and both reports.
